children: Uganda’s initial oil revenues could offer a boost to taxation, debt, foreign currency reserves and country creditworthiness ratings over the short term on the back of new, significant export revenues in spite of uncertainty surrounding the official launch of oil export.

So far, the country’s crude oil product has been branded “Pearl crude” while the 1,445 kilometre East African Crude Oil Pipeline (Eacop) that links Tanga Port in Tanzania to Hoima district of Uganda 92 percent complete, according to government officials.

The Kingfisher oil project run by China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) is scheduled to kick start commercial oil production before end of this year while the Tilenga oil project managed by Total Energies of France is expected to commence oil production in the first quarter of 2027.

Initial oil production volumes pegged to the Kingfisher project are estimated at 25,000 barrels per day. The Kingfisher and Tilenga oil projects are located in the Albertine region of Western Uganda, a vast natural resource area that accommodates roughly 400 oil wells, endangered wildlife species plus Lake Albert- a major fishing zone that connects Uganda to the Eastern part of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Commercial oil production is projected to yield Ush1.5 trillion ($388 million) in initial, government revenues during financial year 2026/27 amidst frequent volatility experienced in the global crude oil market.
The debt-to-GDP ratio stood at 52 percent by end of financial year 2025/26, a figure that exceeds the East African Community (EAC) convergence ceiling of 50 percent of national GDP.

The local current account deficit grew to $3.6 billion by close of financial year 2025/26, a consequence of massive imports of equipment shipped into Uganda by companies engaged in oil and gas related projects since last year.

The value of Uganda’s foreign currency reserves increased by $2.4 billion to $6.7 billion by end of financial year 2025/26, a figure equivalent to 3.7 months of imports of goods and services required under emergency situations.
However, this portfolio valuation falls short of the EAC convergence target of 4.5 months of imports of goods and services contained in the monetary union establishment protocols.
A look at the country’s balance of payments reveals a surplus of $2.4 billion for the period June 2025 to June 2026 according to latest Bank of Uganda data.
A ‘B’ sovereign credit rating accompanied by a stable outlook was issued by Fitch on August 7, 2026, a reflection of modest economic performance indicators and slightly upbeat growth forecasts.

Overall Foreign Direct Investment flows grossed $3,241.8 million between June 2025 and June 2026 on account of considerable foreign capital pumped into the oil and gas sector.“The entry of oil production revenues in our budgeting system will help pay off some external debt contracted earlier on and this will improve on our debt to GDP ratio in the short term. The tax to GDP ratio will also improve on account of fresh tax revenues indirectly generated from oil and gas production. Inflows of new oil and gas revenues will expand our foreign currency reserves in the short term and minimise BOU’s intervention dilemma in the foreign exchange market,” explained Musa Mayanja Lwanga, an economist.“The debt to GDP ratio will improve in the short term because of reduced borrowing pressures anticipated after receipt of first oil revenues. Our tax to GDP ratio will also improve on the weight of new oil revenues. Foreign currency reserves will equally increase but oil revenues cannot fix all our economic problems. Oil production will directly boost our sovereign credit ratings in the short term but issues of political governance, fiscal accountability and quality project execution cannot be ignored. For example, implementation of large, ongoing transport projects that are running behind schedule and beyond budget will affect Uganda’s credit ratings inspite of oil export revenues,” explained Dr Brian Serunjongi, a senior research fellow at the Economic Policy Research Centre based at Makerere University.
